title: Reversibility and detailed balance
objectives: Check detailed balance and recognise a reversible chain
Find a stationary distribution by balancing neighbours
Tell reversible chains from chains that only have a stationary distribution

screens.title: Count the switches
screens.prose: The regime chain sits at its stationary split. Over 1,500 consecutive days, about 1,000 are bull and 500 are bear. Count the switches in each direction.
screens.question: Fill in the expected number of each kind of switch.

rows: A bull day, then a bear day
A bear day, then a bull day

hints.text: About 1,000 days are bull. What fraction of them are followed by a bear day?
Only the 1,000 bull days can switch to bear. Only the 500 bear days can switch to bull.
Bull then bear: $1{,}000 \times 0.1$. Bear then bull: $500 \times 0.2$.

feedback.correct: Both switches happen about 100 times in 1,500 days.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the days in the starting state, then apply that state's switch chance.

byKey.r0c1: Only the 1,000 bull days can switch to bear. Apply 0.1 to 1,000, not to all 1,500 days.
byKey.r1c1: A bear-to-bull switch starts on one of the 500 bear days. Apply 0.2 to 500.

explain.text: About 1,000 bull days switch with chance 0.1, giving 100. About 500 bear days switch with chance 0.2, giving 100. The two flows match.

screens.title: Name the balance
screens.prose: Write each flow as an entry $F_{ij} = \pi_iP_{ij}$. The two switches have equal flow: $\pi_iP_{ij} = \pi_jP_{ji}$. We call this **detailed balance**. A chain with such a $\pi$ is **reversible**: filmed and run backwards, it looks the same.

state.caption: $F_{ij} = \pi_iP_{ij}$: the share of days in state $i$ followed by state $j$.

screens.question: In the backward film, what share of days is a bull day followed by a bear day?

hints.text: Run the film backwards. A bear day followed by a bull day becomes a bull day followed by a bear day.
So the backward share of bull then bear is the forward share of bear then bull.
That is $F_{\text{Bear},\text{Bull}} = \tfrac13 \times 0.2 = \tfrac1{15}$.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac1{15} \approx 0.0667$, the same as the forward share.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read a share of all days from the matrix $F$, not a transition chance.

byKey.transition: You used the transition chance 0.1. The matrix holds shares of all days, which already include $\pi_{\text{Bull}}$.
byKey.swapped: You used the bear-to-bull chance 0.2 as a share. Multiply it by the bear share $\tfrac13$ first.
byKey.both: You added the two switches. The backward film swaps their roles but does not double them.

explain.text: A backward film turns each bear-then-bull switch into a bull-then-bear switch. Both flows are $\tfrac1{15}$, so the backward film has the same switching rates as the forward one. That is what reversible means.

screens.title: Balance between neighbours
screens.prose: A market maker holds 0 to 3 lots. Each step they buy one lot with chance 0.3 or sell one with chance 0.5, and otherwise hold. They never go below 0 or above 3. Assume the long-run flow up from $i$ lots matches the flow back down from $i + 1$.

state.caption: Flow up from 1 lot against flow down from 2 lots.

screens.question: Find the ratio $\pi_{i+1}/\pi_i$.

hints.text: Write the flow up from $i$ and the flow down from $i + 1$. Each is a share times a chance.
Flow up is $\pi_i \times 0.3$. Flow down is $\pi_{i+1} \times 0.5$.
Set $0.3\pi_i = 0.5\pi_{i+1}$ and divide by $\pi_i$ and 0.5.

feedback.correct: $\pi_{i+1} = 0.6\,\pi_i$: each extra lot is 0.6 times as likely as the one below.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Equate $\pi_i \times 0.3$ with $\pi_{i+1} \times 0.5$, then solve for the ratio.

byKey.inverted: You divided the other way. The flow up is $0.3\pi_i$ and the flow down is $0.5\pi_{i+1}$, so $\pi_{i+1}$ is the smaller one.
byKey.buy-only: That is the chance of buying. The ratio compares two flows: $0.3\pi_i = 0.5\pi_{i+1}$.
byKey.sell-only: That is the chance of selling. The ratio compares two flows: $0.3\pi_i = 0.5\pi_{i+1}$.
byKey.difference: You subtracted the two chances. Balance sets two products equal, so we divide, not subtract.

explain.text: Balance gives $0.3\pi_i = 0.5\pi_{i+1}$, so $\pi_{i+1} = \tfrac{0.3}{0.5}\pi_i = 0.6\pi_i$. Selling is more likely than buying, so larger inventories are rarer.

screens.title: Weights, then a total
screens.prose: Give state 0 the weight $w_0 = 1$. Each step up multiplies the weight by 0.6, so $w_1 = 0.6$. Fill in the rest, and the total.

state.caption: We scale the weights to a total of 1 afterwards.

screens.question: Complete the weights.

hints.text: Each weight is the one below it, times 0.6.
State 2 has weight $0.6 \times 0.6$.
$w_2 = 0.36$ and $w_3 = 0.36 \times 0.6$. Add all four.

feedback.correct: The weights are $1, 0.6, 0.36, 0.216$, and they add to 2.176.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the previous weight by 0.6 each time, then add all four weights.

byKey.r2c1: Each step multiplies by 0.6 again, so $w_2 = 0.6 \times w_1 = 0.36$, not 0.6 or 1.2.
byKey.r3c1: Each step multiplies by 0.6 again, so $w_3 = 0.6 \times w_2 = 0.216$, not 0.6 or 1.8.
byKey.r4c1: The total includes all four weights, with $w_0 = 1$ as well.

explain.text: The weights are the powers of 0.6: $1, 0.6, 0.36, 0.216$. Their total is $2.176$. Dividing each weight by 2.176 makes the shares add to 1.

screens.title: Normalise
screens.prose: Divide each weight by the total 2.176 to get $\pi$. Then ask how often the market maker is long two lots or more.
screens.question: What is the long-run chance of holding 2 or 3 lots?

hints.text: Add the shares of state 2 and state 3.
Use the shares, not the weights: divide by 2.176 first.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the weights of states 2 and 3, then divide by 2.176.

byKey.unscaled: You added the weights 0.36 and 0.216 but did not divide by the total 2.176.
byKey.two-only: That is state 2 alone. Add state 3 as well.
byKey.weights-over-4: You divided by 4, the number of states. Divide by the total weight, 2.176.
byKey.half: You counted two of four states. The states are not equally likely.

screens.title: Balance implies stationary
screens.prose: Why does balancing neighbours work? Suppose $\pi_iP_{ij} = \pi_jP_{ji}$ for every pair and $\sum_i \pi_i = 1$. We show that $\pi P = \pi$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: $\pi_iP_{ij} = \pi_jP_{ji}$ for all $i, j$: detailed balance, assumed
$\sum_i \pi_iP_{ij} = \sum_i \pi_jP_{ji}$: sum both sides over every state $i$

hints.text: Start from the assumption, then sum over the first index.
After summing, pull $\pi_j$ out of the sum on the right.
Assumption, sum, factor, row sums to 1, conclusion.

feedback.correct: Balance for every pair gives balance for each column, which is $\pi P = \pi$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with the assumed balance, and finish with the column equation.

byKey.o2: The sum comes straight after the assumption, because there is nothing to sum before it.
byKey.o3: Pulling out $\pi_j$ needs the summed line first.
byKey.o4: The row sum is used after $\pi_j$ has been pulled out of the sum.
byKey.o5: The conclusion is the last line.

explain.text: Summing the pairwise balances over $i$ turns the right side into $\pi_j$, because a row of $P$ adds to 1. The left side is column $j$ of $\pi P$. So $\pi P = \pi$, and a balanced $\pi$ that adds to 1 is stationary.

screens.title: Birth-death chains
screens.prose: A **birth-death chain** moves only to a neighbouring state, or stays. Pairs that are not neighbours have $P = 0$ both ways, so balance holds for them at once. Every such chain on a finite set of states is reversible, with $$\pi_{i+1} = \pi_i\,\frac{P_{i,i+1}}{P_{i+1,i}}.$$
screens.question: A walker on states 0 to 5 moves up with chance 0.6 and down with chance 0.1. It holds still if a move would leave the range. Which is true?

options.why: You inverted the ratio. Flow up is $0.6\pi_i$ and flow down is $0.1\pi_{i+1}$, so $\pi_{i+1}$ is the larger.

options.text: It is not reversible, because it drifts upward
options.why: You read drift as a lack of reversibility. At the wall, probability piles up until flow down matches flow up.

options.text: It is reversible only if the up and down chances are equal
options.why: That is the symmetric case, with uniform $\pi$. The inventory chain had unequal chances and was reversible too.

feedback.correct: Between neighbours $0.6\pi_i = 0.1\pi_{i+1}$, so each state is 6 times as likely as the one below.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\pi_{i+1} = \pi_i P_{i,i+1}/P_{i+1,i}$ with the two chances.

explain.text: The ratio is $0.6 / 0.1 = 6$. The walker drifts up, so probability sits at the top. Still, the flow up from $i$ equals the flow down from $i + 1$, so the chain is reversible.

screens.title: Stationary is not reversible
screens.prose: A rule rotates through venues A, B and C: clockwise with chance 0.8, anticlockwise with chance 0.2. A colleague solves $\pi P = \pi$ and gets $\pi = (\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)$. She says detailed balance must hold.
screens.question: Compare the flows A to B and B to A. What follows?

options.text: A to B is 0.267 and B to A is 0.067. It is stationary but not reversible
The flows balance, because every stationary distribution satisfies detailed balance
options.why: You assumed stationarity forces balance pair by pair. Here probability circulates: A to B is 0.267 and B to A is 0.067.

options.text: Then $\pi$ is not stationary, because the flows differ
options.why: You mixed up stationary and reversible. Each state still receives as much as it sends, so $\pi P = \pi$ holds.

options.text: It is reversible, because the three shares are equal
options.why: Equal shares do not test anything. Compare $\pi_AP_{AB}$ with $\pi_BP_{BA}$.

hints.text: Work out the flow from A to B: the share at A times the chance of going to B.
Do the same for B to A. Clockwise is 0.8 and anticlockwise is 0.2.
$\tfrac13 \times 0.8$ against $\tfrac13 \times 0.2$.

feedback.correct: Flows 0.267 and 0.067 differ, so the chain is not reversible. It is still stationary.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find both flows, then ask separately whether they match and whether $\pi P = \pi$ holds.

byKey.always: You assumed stationarity forces balance pair by pair. Here probability circulates: A to B is 0.267 and B to A is 0.067.
byKey.notstat: You mixed up stationary and reversible. Each state still receives as much as it sends, so $\pi P = \pi$ holds.
byKey.equal: Equal shares do not test anything. Compare $\pi_AP_{AB}$ with $\pi_BP_{BA}$.

explain.text: The flow from A to B is $\tfrac13 \times 0.8 = 0.267$, and from B to A it is $\tfrac13 \times 0.2 = 0.067$. Probability circulates, yet each state's inflow equals its outflow, so $\pi P = \pi$. Detailed balance is a stronger condition than stationarity.

screens.title: Balance has no solution
screens.prose: Try detailed balance on the same cycle. A to B gives $0.8\pi_A = 0.2\pi_B$, so $\pi_B = 4\pi_A$. B to C gives $\pi_C = 4\pi_B$. C to A gives $\pi_A = 4\pi_C$.
screens.question: Going round the cycle, $\pi_A$ must equal how many times itself?

hints.text: Substitute $\pi_C = 4\pi_B$ and $\pi_B = 4\pi_A$ into $\pi_A = 4\pi_C$.
Each of the three steps multiplies by 4.
$\pi_A = 4 \times 4 \times 4\,\pi_A$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the three factors of 4 together.

byKey.twelve: You added the three 4s. Each equation multiplies, so the factors multiply.
byKey.three: You counted the steps. Each step contributes a factor of 4.
byKey.one: That would be consistent. Check: each step multiplies by 4, so the product is not 1.

explain.text: Going round gives $\pi_A = 4 \times 4 \times 4\,\pi_A = 64\pi_A$. That forces $\pi_A = 0$, so there is no balanced distribution. When balance has no solution, solve $\pi P = \pi$ instead.

screens.title: One-way arrows
screens.prose: An arrow with no arrow back is a one-way edge: $P_{ij} > 0$ but $P_{ji} = 0$. Balance would need $\pi_iP_{ij} = \pi_j \times 0$.
screens.question: Tap every arrow that rules out reversibility.

hints.text: Look for a pair of states with an arrow one way and none back.
A and B have arrows both ways. Check B and C, then C and A.
B goes to C but C never goes to B. C goes to A but A never goes to C.

feedback.correct: B to C and C to A each lack a return arrow.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap only arrows whose reverse arrow is missing.

byKey.pair: A and B have arrows in both directions, so that pair can balance.
byKey.all: The A and B arrows come as a pair. Only arrows without a return arrow count.
byKey.e-A-B: A to B has a return arrow B to A.
byKey.e-B-A: B to A has a return arrow A to B.

explain.text: $P_{BC} = 0.2$ but $P_{CB} = 0$, so balance needs $0.2\pi_B = 0$, which forces $\pi_B = 0$. A chain that visits B has no such $\pi$. Every arrow in a reversible chain needs a return arrow.

screens.title: An order queue
screens.prose: Orders queue at the best bid, up to 3 in the model. Each step a new order joins with chance 0.3. A queued order leaves, filled or cancelled, with chance 0.6.

state.caption: Orders queued at the best bid, capped at 3.

screens.question: What share of the time is the queue empty?

hints.text: Balance neighbours: joining at rate 0.3 against leaving at rate 0.6.
The ratio is $0.3/0.6 = 0.5$, so the weights are $1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125$.
Divide $1$ by the total weight $1.875$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the weights, add all four, and divide the first by the total.

byKey.ratio-only: You used the ratio 0.5 as the share. Normalise: the weights $1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125$ add to 1.875.
byKey.three-states: You left out the fourth state. The weights are $1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125$ and add to 1.875.
byKey.point-six: That is the chance a queued order leaves. The share of time empty comes from the weights.
byKey.quarter: You split the time evenly over four states. A longer queue is less likely.

explain.text: Balance gives $\pi_{i+1} = 0.5\pi_i$, so $\pi = (8, 4, 2, 1)/15$ and the queue is empty 53% of the time. A market order arriving then walks past the best bid, which is why the market maker cares.

ideas: Detailed balance, $\pi_iP_{ij} = \pi_jP_{ji}$ for every pair, means the flows match both ways. A chain with such a $\pi$ is reversible.
A $\pi$ that satisfies detailed balance and adds to 1 is stationary: sum the equations over $i$. Birth-death chains on a finite set of states are always reversible.
Stationary does not imply reversible. A cycle that circulates has a stationary $\pi$ but unequal flows, and a one-way arrow rules out reversibility.
summary.trap: Solving $\pi P = \pi$ always works. Detailed balance can have no solution, so check it before trusting it.

quiz.prose: A queue holds 0, 1 or 2 orders. Per step it grows by one with chance 0.2 or shrinks by one with chance 0.4. It never leaves 0 to 2.
quiz.question: What is the long-run chance the queue is empty?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each state has half the weight of the one below, then normalise.

byKey.equal: You split the time evenly. Larger queues are rarer.
byKey.ratio: You used the ratio 0.5 as the share. Divide 1 by the total weight 1.75.
byKey.second: That is the share at 1 order. Empty is the largest weight.

explain.text: Balance gives $0.2\pi_i = 0.4\pi_{i+1}$, so the weights are $1, 0.5, 0.25$ with total $1.75$. Then $\pi_0 = 1/1.75 = \tfrac47 \approx 0.5714$.

quiz.prose: A chain on three states has flow matrix $F_{ij} = \pi_iP_{ij}$ equal to $$F = \begin{pmatrix}\tfrac16 & \tfrac16 & 0\\ 0 & \tfrac16 & \tfrac16\\ \tfrac16 & 0 & \tfrac16\end{pmatrix}.$$ Each row and each column adds to $\tfrac13$.
quiz.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: It is stationary but not reversible, because $F$ is not symmetric
It is reversible, because every row adds to $\tfrac13$
options.why: Equal row sums say $\pi$ is uniform. Reversible means $F$ equals its transpose.

options.text: It is not stationary, because $F$ is not symmetric
options.why: Stationary needs row sums to equal column sums, which they do. Symmetry is the stronger test for reversible.

options.text: It is reversible, because no entry is negative
options.why: Non-negative entries hold for every chain. Compare $F_{12}$ with $F_{21}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each entry with the one mirrored across the diagonal.

explain.text: Rows and columns both add to $\tfrac13$, so $\pi = (\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)$ is stationary. But $F_{12} = \tfrac16$ and $F_{21} = 0$. A reversible chain has $F = F^T$.

quiz.prose: Detailed balance is checked for every pair $(i, j)$. A student asks whether the pairs with $i = j$ need checking.
quiz.question: What is the right answer?

options.text: No: for $i = j$ the equation reads $\pi_iP_{ii} = \pi_iP_{ii}$, which always holds
Yes: a state that stays put may break the balance
options.why: You expected staying put to matter. The flow from $i$ to itself is the same number on both sides.
A chain can hold with $P_{ii} > 0$, as the inventory chain did. The equation is simply trivial.

options.text: Yes, but only the states with $P_{ii} > \tfrac12$
options.why: No threshold applies. Both sides are the same product, so the equation is an identity.

feedback.correct: Both sides are the same product, so a self-loop never breaks balance.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the equation with $j = i$ and compare the two sides.

explain.text: With $j = i$, $\pi_iP_{ij} = \pi_jP_{ji}$ becomes $\pi_iP_{ii} = \pi_iP_{ii}$. Only pairs of different states can fail.

quiz.prose: A reversible chain has stationary $\pi = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2)$ and $P_{12} = 0.2$, the chance of moving from state 1 to state 2.
quiz.question: What is $P_{21}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\pi_1P_{12} = \pi_2P_{21}$ and solve for $P_{21}$.

byKey.symmetric: You assumed $P_{21} = P_{12}$. That holds only when $\pi_1 = \pi_2$.
byKey.inverted: You inverted the ratio of shares. State 2 is the rarer one, so its exit chance is larger.
byKey.tiny: You multiplied all three numbers. Divide by $\pi_2$ instead.

explain.text: Balance says $0.5 \times 0.2 = 0.3 \times P_{21}$. So $P_{21} = 0.10 / 0.3 = \tfrac13$. The rarer state 2 must leave faster than state 1.
